title: Chapter 35. Of the Signification in Scripture of Kingdom of God, of Holy, Sacred, and Sacrament
section: Part III — Of a Christian Commonwealth
paragraphs: The Kingdom of God in the writings of divines, and especially in sermons and treatises of devotion, is taken most commonly for eternal felicity after this life, in the highest heaven, which they also call the kingdom of glory; and sometimes for (the earnest of that felicity) sanctification, which they call the kingdom of grace. But it is never taken for monarchy — that is, for the sovereign power of God over subjects acquired by their own consent — which is the proper meaning of 'kingdom.'

On the contrary, I find that the KINGDOM OF GOD signifies, in most places of Scripture, a kingdom properly so called, constituted by the votes of the people of Israel in a peculiar way: in which they chose God for their king by a covenant made with him, on God's promising them the possession of the land of Canaan. And only seldom does it have a metaphorical sense, and then it is taken for dominion over sin (and only in the New Testament), because such a dominion as that, every subject shall have in the kingdom of God, and without prejudice to the sovereign.

From the very creation, God not only reigned over all men naturally by his might; he also had peculiar subjects, whom he commanded by a voice, as one man speaks to another. In that way he reigned over Adam, and gave him a commandment to abstain from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; which when Adam disobeyed but tasted of it, taking upon himself to be as God, judging between good and evil not by his Creator's commandment but by his own sense, his punishment was the deprivation of the state of eternal life in which God had at first created him. And afterwards God punished his posterity, for their vices, all but eight persons, with a universal deluge; and in these eight consisted the kingdom of God at that time.

After this, it pleased God to speak to Abraham, and (Gen. 17:7–8) to make a covenant with him in these words: 'I will establish my covenant between me and you, and your seed after you in their generations, for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you. And I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land in which you are a stranger, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession.' And as a memorial and a token of this covenant, he ordains (verse 11) the sacrament of circumcision. This is what is called the Old Covenant, or Testament, and contains a contract between God and Abraham, by which Abraham obliges himself, and his posterity, in a peculiar way, to be subject to God's positive law — for to the moral law he was obliged already, as by an oath of allegiance. And though the name 'king' is not yet given to God, nor 'kingdom' to Abraham and his seed, the thing is the same: namely, an institution by pact of God's peculiar sovereignty over the seed of Abraham. This in the renewing of the same covenant by Moses at Mount Sinai is expressly called a peculiar kingdom of God over the Jews; and it is of Abraham (not of Moses) that St Paul says (Rom. 4:11) he is the 'father of the faithful' — that is, of those who are loyal, and do not violate their allegiance sworn to God, then by circumcision, and afterwards in the new covenant by baptism.
That the kingdom of God is properly his civil sovereignty over a peculiar people by pact.

This covenant, at the foot of Mount Sinai, was renewed by Moses (Exod. 19:5), where the Lord commands Moses to speak to the people in this way: 'If you will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then you shall be a peculiar people to me, for all the earth is mine; and you shall be to me a sacerdotal kingdom, and a holy nation.' For 'peculiar people,' the Vulgate Latin has peculium de cunctis populis; the English translation made at the beginning of the reign of King James has 'a peculiar treasure unto me above all nations'; and the Geneva French, 'the most precious jewel of all nations.' But the truest translation is the first, because it is confirmed by St Paul himself (Tit. 2:14), where he says, alluding to that place, that our blessed Saviour 'gave himself for us, that he might purify to himself a peculiar (that is, an extraordinary) people.' For the word in the Greek is periousios, which is commonly opposed to the word epiousios; and as epiousios signifies 'ordinary,' 'daily,' or (as in the Lord's Prayer) 'of daily use,' so the other signifies that which is overplus, and stored up, and enjoyed in a special manner — which the Latins call peculium. And this meaning of the passage is confirmed by the reason God gives for it, which follows immediately, when he adds 'For all the earth is mine' — as if he should say: 'All the nations of the world are mine; but it is not so that you are mine, but in a special manner.' For they are all his by reason of his power; but you shall be mine by your own consent and covenant — which is an addition to his ordinary title to all nations.

The same is again confirmed in express words in the same text: 'You shall be to me a sacerdotal kingdom, and a holy nation.' The Vulgate has Regnum Sacerdotale, which agrees with the translation of that passage (1 Pet. 2:9) Sacerdotium Regale, a 'royal priesthood'; as also with the institution itself, by which no man might enter into the Sanctum Sanctorum — that is, no man might inquire of God's will immediately from God himself — except the high priest only. The English translation already mentioned, following that of Geneva, has 'a kingdom of priests,' which is either meant of the succession of one high priest after another, or else it does not accord with St Peter, nor with the exercise of the high priesthood. For there was never any but the high priest only who was to inform the people of God's will; nor was any convocation of priests ever allowed to enter into the Sanctum Sanctorum.

Again, the title of a 'holy nation' confirms the same. For 'holy' signifies that which is God's by special, not by general, right. All the earth (as is said in the text) is God's; but all the earth is not called holy — only that which is set apart for his special service, as the nation of the Jews was. It is therefore plain enough by this one passage that by the kingdom of God is properly meant a commonwealth, instituted (by the consent of those who were to be subject to it) for their civil government, and for the regulating of their behaviour not only toward God their king, but also toward one another in point of justice, and toward other nations both in peace and in war; which was properly a kingdom, in which God was king and the high priest was to be (after the death of Moses) his sole viceroy, or lieutenant.

But there are many other places that clearly prove the same. First (1 Sam. 8:7), when the elders of Israel (grieved by the corruption of the sons of Samuel) demanded a king, Samuel was displeased with this, and prayed to the Lord; and the Lord, answering, said to him: 'Listen to the voice of the people, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.' From which it is evident that God himself was then their king; and that Samuel did not command the people, but only delivered to them what God from time to time appointed him.

Again, (1 Sam. 12:12), where Samuel says to the people: 'When you saw that Nahash, king of the children of Ammon, came against you, you said to me, Nay, but a king shall reign over us — when the Lord your God was your king.' It is plain that God was their king, and governed the civil state of their commonwealth.

And after the Israelites had rejected God, the prophets foretold his restoration. As in Isaiah 24:23: 'Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the Lord of hosts shall reign in Mount Zion, and in Jerusalem' — where he speaks expressly of his reign in Zion and Jerusalem; that is, on earth. And (Micah 4:7), 'And the Lord shall reign over them in Mount Zion'; this Mount Zion is in Jerusalem, on the earth. And (Ezek. 20:33), 'As I live, says the Lord God, surely with a mighty hand, and a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out, I will rule over you'; and (verse 37) 'I will cause you to pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant' — that is, 'I will reign over you, and make you stand to that covenant which you made with me by Moses, and broke in your rebellion against me in the days of Samuel, and in your election of another king.'

And in the New Testament, the angel Gabriel says of our Saviour (Luke 1:32–33): 'He shall be great, and be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord shall give him the throne of his father David; and he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end.' This is also a kingdom on earth; for the claim of which, as an enemy to Caesar, he was put to death. The title of his cross was 'Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews'; he was crowned in scorn with a crown of thorns; and for the proclaiming of him it is said of the disciples (Acts 17:7) that 'they did all of them contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying there was another king, one Jesus.' The kingdom therefore of God is a real, not a metaphorical, kingdom — and so taken not only in the Old Testament but in the New. When we say, 'For yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory,' it is to be understood of God's kingdom by force of our covenant, not by the right of God's power; for such a kingdom God always has. So it would be superfluous to say in our prayer, 'Your kingdom come,' unless it is meant of the restoration of that kingdom of God by Christ which by the revolt of the Israelites had been interrupted at the election of Saul. Nor would it have been proper to say 'The kingdom of heaven is at hand,' or to pray 'Your kingdom come,' if it had still continued.

There are so many other places that confirm this interpretation that it would be a wonder no greater notice is taken of it — except that it gives too much light to Christian kings to see their right of ecclesiastical government. This is what those have observed who, in place of 'sacerdotal kingdom,' translate 'a kingdom of priests'; for they may as well translate 'royal priesthood' (as it is in St Peter) into 'a priesthood of kings.' And whereas, for 'peculiar people,' they put 'precious jewel,' or 'treasure,' a man might as well call the special regiment, or company, of a general the general's 'precious jewel,' or his 'treasure.'

In short, the kingdom of God is a civil kingdom; which consisted first in the obligation of the people of Israel to those laws which Moses should bring to them from Mount Sinai, and which afterwards the high priest of the time being should deliver to them from before the cherubim in the Sanctum Sanctorum; and which kingdom, having been cast off at the election of Saul, the prophets foretold should be restored by Christ. And the restoration of it we daily pray for, when we say in the Lord's Prayer, 'Your kingdom come'; and the right of it we acknowledge, when we add, 'For yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory, for ever and ever, amen'; and the proclaiming of it was the preaching of the apostles. To which men are prepared by the teachers of the gospel; to embrace which gospel (that is, to promise obedience to God's government) is to be in the kingdom of grace, because God has gratis given to such the power to be the subjects (that is, children) of God hereafter, when Christ shall come in majesty to judge the world, and actually to govern his own people — which is called the kingdom of glory. If the kingdom of God (also called the kingdom of heaven, from the gloriousness and admirable height of that throne) were not a kingdom which God, by his lieutenant or vicars, who deliver his commandments to the people, did exercise on earth, there would not have been so much contention and war about who it is by whom God speaks to us; nor would many priests have troubled themselves with spiritual jurisdiction, nor any king have denied it to them.

Out of this literal interpretation of the kingdom of God arises also the true interpretation of the word HOLY. For it is a word which in God's kingdom answers to that which men in their kingdoms use to call 'public,' or 'the king's.'

The king of any country is the public person, or representative, of all his own subjects. And God, the king of Israel, was the Holy One of Israel. The nation which is subject to one earthly sovereign is the nation of that sovereign — that is, of the public person. So the Jews, who were God's nation, were called (Exod. 19:6) 'a holy nation.' For by 'holy' is always understood either God himself, or what is God's in property; as by 'public' is always meant either the person of the commonwealth itself, or something that is so the commonwealth's that no private person can claim any property in it.

Therefore the Sabbath (God's day) is a holy day; the temple (God's house) a holy house; sacrifices, tithes, and offerings (God's tribute) holy duties; priests, prophets, and anointed kings under Christ (God's ministers) holy men; the celestial ministering spirits (God's messengers) holy angels; and the like. Wherever the word 'holy' is taken properly, there is always signified something of property, gotten by consent. In saying 'Hallowed be your name,' we do but pray to God for grace to keep the first commandment, of 'having no other gods but Him.' Mankind is God's nation in general, but the Jews only were a holy nation. Why? Because they became his property by covenant.

And the word 'profane' is usually taken in Scripture for the same as 'common'; and consequently their contraries, 'holy' and 'proper,' in the kingdom of God must be the same also. But figuratively, those men too are called holy who led such godly lives that it was as though they had forsaken all worldly designs, and wholly devoted, and given, themselves to God. In the proper sense, what is made holy by God's appropriating or separating it to his own use is said to be sanctified by God — as the seventh day in the fourth commandment; and as the elect in the New Testament were said to be sanctified when they were endowed with the spirit of godliness. And what is made holy by the dedication of men, and given to God so as to be used only in his public service, is also called SACRED, and said to be consecrated — as temples and other houses of public prayer, and their utensils, priests, and ministers, victims, offerings, and the external matter of the sacraments.

Of holiness there are degrees. For of those things set apart for the service of God, some may be set apart again, for a nearer and more especial service. The whole nation of the Israelites were a people holy to God; yet the tribe of Levi was, among the Israelites, a holy tribe; and among the Levites, the priests were yet more holy; and among the priests, the high priest was the most holy. So the land of Judea was the Holy Land; but the holy city in which God was to be worshipped was more holy; and again, the temple more holy than the city; and the Sanctum Sanctorum more holy than the rest of the temple.

A SACRAMENT is a setting apart of some visible thing from common use, and a consecration of it to God's service, for a sign — either of our admission into the kingdom of God, to be of the number of his peculiar people, or as a commemoration of the same. In the Old Testament, the sign of admission was circumcision; in the New Testament, baptism. The commemoration of it in the Old Testament was the eating (at a certain time, which was annual) of the paschal lamb, by which they were reminded of the night in which they were delivered out of their bondage in Egypt; and in the New Testament, the celebrating of the Lord's Supper, by which we are reminded of our deliverance from the bondage of sin, by our blessed Saviour's death on the cross. The sacraments of admission are to be used only once, because only one admission is needed; but because we have need of being often reminded of our deliverance, and of our allegiance, the sacraments of commemoration need to be repeated. These are the principal sacraments — as it were, the solemn oaths we make of our allegiance. There are also other consecrations that may be called sacraments, as the word implies only consecration to God's service; but as it implies an oath, or promise, of allegiance to God, there were no others in the Old Testament except circumcision and the Passover, nor are there any others in the New Testament except baptism and the Lord's Supper.
